title: THE ULTIMATE TEST OF EVERY CHRISTIAN TEACHER: AFTER LISTENING TO THEM, WHO DO YOU WANT MORE—JESUS OR THEM?
paragraphs: THE ULTIMATE TEST OF EVERY CHRISTIAN TEACHER: AFTER LISTENING TO THEM, WHO DO YOU WANT MORE—JESUS OR THEM?

The most dangerous spiritual deception may not be the teacher who tells you to abandon Christ, but the teacher who keeps saying “Jesus” while slowly teaching your heart to revolve around a human personality.
There is a question almost nobody asks after the sermon ends.
Not, “Was that preacher powerful?”
Not, “Did I enjoy the message?”
Not, “How many followers does this ministry have?”
Not even, “Did I learn something new?”
The question is far more uncomfortable.
Where did they just lead me?
Toward Jesus?
Or toward themselves?
Because it is possible to speak about Jesus while quietly building fascination with the messenger.
It is possible to hold a Bible and still cultivate a personality cult.
It is possible to preach truth while becoming addicted to applause.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility of all is this:
A Christian teacher can begin by sincerely wanting people to know Christ…and somewhere along the road begin needing those same people to need them.
That should make every preacher tremble.
Including me.
Including anyone who teaches Scripture.
Including the person whose ministry you love most.
The Bible gives us an astonishingly simple sentence by which Christian influence can be measured.
John the Baptist said:
“ἐκεῖνον δεῖ αὐξάνειν, ἐμὲ δὲ ἐλαττοῦσθαι.”
Ekeînon deî auxánein, emè dè elattoûsthai.
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
—John 3:30
Look closely at the word δεῖ — deî.
It carries the sense of necessity.
It must happen.
Christ must increase.
John must decrease.
And that sentence becomes devastating when you remember who John was.
Crowds had come to him.
People listened to him.
He had disciples.
He had influence.
Jesus Himself would speak extraordinarily highly of him.
Yet when John saw attention beginning to move toward Jesus, he did not panic because his platform was shrinking.
He rejoiced.
That is the heart of a true servant.
John understood something our celebrity-obsessed age desperately needs to recover:
The purpose of the messenger is not to make people unable to live without the messenger. The purpose of the messenger is to bring people to the Messiah.

A faithful Christian teacher should leave you increasingly dependent upon Christ, increasingly hungry for Scripture, increasingly sensitive to sin, increasingly grateful for grace, increasingly committed to prayer, increasingly willing to obey Jesus when obedience costs you something.
You may appreciate the teacher.
You may honor them.
You may learn from them.
You may support their ministry.
Scripture itself recognizes and honors faithful spiritual leadership.

But something has gone terribly wrong when admiration becomes spiritual dependency…when questions become forbidden…when disagreement becomes betrayal…when the teacher becomes practically untouchable…and when Jesus slowly becomes the supporting character in someone else’s ministry.
Paul gave the church an extraordinarily clear standard:
“οὐ γὰρ ἑαυτοὺς κηρύσσομεν ἀλλὰ Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν Κύριον.”
Ou gar heautoùs kēryssomen, allà Christòn Iēsoûn Kýrion.
“For we do not proclaim ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord.”
—2 Corinthians 4:5
Read those words again.
οὐ…ἑαυτοὺς — not ourselves.
ἀλλὰ Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν — but Christ Jesus.
That is not merely a preaching technique.
That is a spiritual dividing line.
Paul does not present himself as the destination.
He presents Christ.
The messenger is a servant.
Jesus is Lord.

And that means the ultimate test of Christian teaching is not merely whether a teacher is charismatic, intelligent, emotional, successful, controversial, traditional, modern, conservative, popular, unpopular, eloquent, scholarly, prophetic-sounding, or capable of quoting Scripture from memory.
The deeper question remains:
What happens to Jesus in the hearts of the people listening?
Does He become greater?
Does the cross become more precious?
Does repentance become more urgent?
Does grace become more astonishing?
Does Scripture become more treasured?
Does holiness become more desirable?
Does the believer become more capable of following Jesus even when the teacher is nowhere around?
Or does the teacher become greater?
Their opinions become unquestionable.
Their personality becomes the attraction.
Their controversies become everyone's obsession.
Their enemies become your enemies.
Their approval becomes emotionally necessary.
Their name dominates your conversations.
Their voice begins carrying more practical authority in your life than the Word they claim to teach.
This danger is not new.
The Corinthian church was already dividing itself around human personalities.
“I follow Paul.”
“I follow Apollos.”
“I follow Cephas.”
Paul’s response was essentially to shatter the entire celebrity mentality with one question:
“Is Christ divided?”
Think about that.
Christians were turning servants into banners.
Paul refused the throne they were trying to build for him.
Later he explained that he and Apollos were servants through whom the Corinthians believed. One planted. Another watered.
But God gave the growth.
That destroys Christian celebrity worship at the root.
The preacher cannot resurrect you.
The pastor cannot cleanse your sin.
The evangelist cannot reconcile you to God.
The author cannot regenerate your heart.
The worship leader cannot carry your guilt.
The influencer cannot stand between you and divine judgment.
And the ministry you love did not bleed on Calvary for you.
Jesus did.
There was only one sinless body nailed to that cross.
There was only one Lamb of God bearing sin.
There was only one Savior who walked out of the grave victorious.
There is only one Mediator between God and humanity.
There is only one name by which we must be saved.
Jesus Christ.
And somewhere reading this right now is a person who has been wounded by someone who carried His name.
Maybe that is you.
You trusted a pastor.
You admired a teacher.
You believed someone because they sounded so certain.
Then you discovered hypocrisy.
Manipulation.
Money.
Control.
Sexual sin.
Pride.
Dishonesty.
Abuse of authority.
Or simply a private character that looked nothing like the public sermon.
Something collapsed inside you.
And perhaps you whispered:
“If that is Christianity, I want nothing to do with it.”
Please hear this carefully.
The failure of a messenger does not invalidate the perfection of the Messiah.
Jesus never told you that every Christian leader would be trustworthy.
In fact, Scripture repeatedly warns you to exercise discernment.
Christ warned about false prophets.
Paul warned the Ephesian elders that distortion could arise even from among themselves.
Acts 20:30 contains an especially chilling expression. Paul warns that men would arise speaking distorted things:
“τοῦ ἀποσπᾶν τοὺς μαθητὰς ὀπίσω ἑαυτῶν.”
The purpose described is to draw away the disciples after themselves.
There it is.
Disciples after themselves.
That is the counterfeit direction.
A faithful teacher says, in effect:
“Follow Christ.”
A corrupting influence eventually says, whether openly or subtly:
“Follow Christ through me…and eventually, do not question me.”
Those are not the same thing.
This is also why discernment cannot mean cynicism.
We must not respond by assuming every large ministry is corrupt or every small ministry is pure.
Numbers prove almost nothing about faithfulness.
Large audiences can hear truth.
Small audiences can hear error.
A wealthy preacher can be faithful.
A poor preacher can be proud.
A polished communicator can love Jesus deeply.
An unpolished communicator can manipulate people terribly.
The test is not aesthetic.
The test runs deeper:
Are they faithfully pointing people toward the biblical Christ rather than making themselves the center?
That question must also turn toward us.
Because it is easy to read an article about false teachers and immediately think of somebody else.
“That pastor.”
“That denomination.”
“That YouTuber.”
“That ministry.”
“That preacher I cannot stand.”
But Scripture has a way of turning the mirror around.
What if you secretly want to be seen?
What if I do?
What if we speak about Jesus partly because we love Jesus…and partly because we love what happens when people applaud us for speaking about Jesus?
That mixture is terrifying.
You can crave recognition while quoting verses about humility.
You can defend sound doctrine while enjoying humiliating people who disagree.
You can post about Christ and refresh the screen repeatedly to see how many people noticed you.
You can build a ministry around the crucified Savior while protecting your own ego as though it must never be crucified.
You can sing, “All glory to God,” and quietly ache when nobody remembers your name.
This article cannot merely judge teachers.
It must judge the heart writing it.
It must judge the heart reading it.
Because every Christian who influences another human being faces some version of this temptation.
Parents.
Pastors.
Bible teachers.
Authors.
Content creators.
Small-group leaders.
Worship leaders.
Apologists.
Evangelists.
Friends discipling friends.
Every one of us eventually faces the same question:
Do I want people impressed with me, or transformed by Christ?
Those two desires can live frighteningly close together.
And sometimes only God knows which one is driving us.
That is why John’s words are not merely beautiful.
They are surgery.
He must increase. I must decrease.
Decrease my ego.
Decrease my hunger for applause.
Decrease my obsession with being recognized.
Decrease my need to win every argument.
Decrease the part of me that wants people quoting my words more than opening Your Word.
Decrease the part of me that loves ministry success more than secret obedience.
Decrease me until people can see past the messenger and behold the King.
Because Christian ministry was never supposed to manufacture fans.
It was meant to make disciples of Jesus Christ.
And discipleship eventually brings us to a scandal.
The scandal of our own sin.
We discover that the deepest problem is not merely manipulative teachers somewhere on the internet.
The rebellion is also inside us.
Pride.
Lust.
Greed.
Bitterness.
Self-righteousness.
Envy.
Secret compromise.
Religious performance.
The desperate human instinct to make ourselves the center.
And Christianity does not tell us to repair that heart through positive thinking.
The Gospel announces something infinitely more costly and infinitely more beautiful.
God came for sinners.
Jesus Christ entered our brokenness.
He lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The answer to corrupt spiritual authority is not abandoning Christ.
The answer to hypocrisy is not abandoning Christ.
The answer to religious trauma is not replacing Jesus with another human savior.
The answer is to return to the One whom every faithful teacher was supposed to point toward in the first place.
Jesus.
Look at Him again.
Not the preacher.
Not the scandal.
Not the institution.
Not the personality.
Christ.
The One who touched lepers when others stepped away.
The One who ate with sinners while religious men complained.
The One who confronted hypocrisy without becoming hypocritical.
The One who possessed all authority yet washed feet.
The One who could have summoned angels yet surrendered Himself to the cross.
The One who knew Peter would deny Him and still restored him.
The One who knew every filthy chapter of your life before you ever learned His name…and still opened His arms at Calvary.
That is our theme because that is the heartbeat of the Gospel:
Not because sin does not matter.
Grace is not God pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace cost blood.
Grace came through a cross.
Grace calls sinners to repentance.
Grace forgives what we could never erase ourselves.
Grace does not merely improve the old story.
In Christ, grace begins rewriting the person.
The proud can become humble.
The sexually broken can learn purity.
The bitter can forgive.
The liar can walk in truth.
The addict can cry out for freedom.
The self-righteous can finally admit, “I need mercy too.”
The wounded believer can discover that Jesus was never identical to the person who misrepresented Him.
The fallen servant can repent rather than hide.
The prodigal can come home.
That is why Jesus must remain the center.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not a pastor.
Not your favorite Christian author.
Not a denomination.
Not me.
Not you.
Jesus.
And yes, ministries need support. Books cost money to produce. Resources cost money to distribute. Platforms cost money to maintain.
But even here, the order matters.
We should never support Christian work because a personality has emotionally cornered us into proving our loyalty.
We support Gospel work because we want Christ proclaimed, believers strengthened, seekers reached, Scripture opened, and the Gospel carried farther.
If you want your resources to help glorify God, one practical way is to support and share work that faithfully proclaims His Son.
But please understand what I am asking you to support.
Not our fame.
Not our name.
Not our ego.
The mission.
Jesus must increase.
We must decrease.
Not merely because sharing helps a page.
Someone may be following a personality more closely than Jesus and not realize it yet.
Someone may have walked away from Christianity because a preacher failed them.
Someone may be sitting alone tonight thinking the hypocrisy they witnessed proves Jesus was a fraud.
Put this article where they might find it.
Because the day may come when a teacher you admire disappoints you, and on that day you will need to remember:
Your faith was never supposed to rest on their perfection.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelievers to follow too—not so that Gospel Warrior becomes the destination, but so that together we can keep pointing one another toward the One who is.
Not publicly at first.
Answer it before God.
When people encounter your Christianity…
who becomes bigger?
Jesus?
Or you?
When you correct someone, do they encounter truth seasoned with the character of Christ—or your need to win?
When you teach, are you building disciples who can stand on Scripture without you—or people emotionally dependent upon your voice?
When God uses you, are you genuinely delighted when people eventually need less of you because they know more of Him?
Could you rejoice if Jesus became famous through your obedience while nobody remembered your name?
That is the test.
Maybe this exposed something uncomfortable in you.
It exposed something in me too.
Then do not hide behind religious language.
Bring it into the light.
Someone reading beneath this article may need the very grace God has already walked you through.
No pretending.
No personality worship.
No hiding.
Just sinners pointing other sinners toward the Savior.
Because one day every platform will disappear.
Every follower count will become meaningless.
Every bestseller list will be forgotten.
Every stage light will go dark.
Every microphone will become silent.
Every ministry name will eventually pass from human memory.
But Jesus Christ will still be King.
So honor faithful teachers.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Support Gospel work.
Hold leaders accountable to Scripture.
Test what you hear.
Refuse cynicism.
Refuse celebrity worship.
And never ask a human shepherd to carry the weight that belongs only to the Good Shepherd.
The best Christian teacher will never make you think, “I cannot survive spiritually without this person.”
They will keep teaching your heart to say:
“I cannot live without Christ.”
That is the destination.
That is the test.
That is the Gospel.
And perhaps the greatest thing that could ever be said about our ministry, our teaching, our writing, our lives, and eventually our graves is not that people remembered our names…
but that because we were here,
someone saw Jesus more clearly.
When every human voice finally goes silent, make sure the Voice your soul learned to follow was Jesus.
